title: How are you handling AI-driven narrative without the output feeling generic?
author: Former-Objective-272
selftext:
I am trying an approach where I write all the story pieces by hand but let AI decide what triggers when and in what order. AI is the conductor, not the composer.

The AI tracks player actions across runs and picks which narrative events to fire. All the actual text is human written. The sequencing is procedural.

Works ok most of the time but occasionally the AI makes choices that fit the logic tree but feel random. Like an NPC acting hostile because of something from 5 runs ago that the player barely remembers.

How do you deal with this? Tighter constraints? Post processing? Curious what tools or approaches others here use for narrative direction.

comments.author: Will_X_Intent
comments.body:
lol you clarified what you meant by the director approach without first mentioning it.  I wonder what kind of AI you even need for a system like that.  Non LLM surely.   You could try to train something, but I dont know how you would design a system so that it could iterate fast enough to learn quickly.  Hand training an AI to make good choices would be hell.  Maybe find an LLM that can be given the ability to "play" the game, and prompt it what a good AI chooser thing would look like.  Like, what is a good outcome for the director to choose.  Then maybe it can play the training game fast.  Maybe.  

It's a really cool idea you got, with a tough engineering problem you must solve to make it real.  But I think it's doable.  

If you succeed, want to combine your game with mine?  I'm building an RPG type thing with an innovative skill system.  They might fit together, who knows.

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body:
Ha fair, I buried the explanation. So the director part is actually not AI at all. It is hand written logic that acts like a film director would: it knows the story beats (main plot is fixed, like the protagonist always dies at a certain point no matter what), and it decides pacing, tone, which subplots to surface.

The AI comes in after the director makes those calls. It takes the fixed mainline plus the director's decisions and generates the branching content around them. Think of the director as the skeleton, AI fills in the muscle.

The matching part is more like vector similarity. We track player behaviors and choices across runs, encode that as a vector, and match against a library of pre written branch templates. The closer the match, the more that branch fits. Not training a model, more like a recommendation engine.

It is a lot of moving parts but honestly the director logic is the easiest bit. The hard part is making sure generated branches dont contradict the main plot.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body:
Are you sure you buried it?  Because I see just a few lines in your original post.   
  
if it's deciding things, and it's not some algorithm, I think that makes it an AI.  (be careful with forcing player death.  It can be used well, but it's tricky).  You are calling it a director like it's choosing, but also saying it's just simple math.  Which is it?  If you can describe it in a flow chart with algorithmic gates, calling it a director is misleading.  It's just complicated math.  

So if it's procedural content generation (kinda), you want the AI to stitch it together to make it make sense?  The brute force way here would be to have AI generate the "muscle" for every possible connection, outside of the game, not at runtime.  

saying the vector matching is the easy part was funny.  Just the fine tuning will probably eat a ton of time.  Let alone finding people to help you properly test it.  But I can kinda see the same.  Kinda like a matrix field, or say, the alignment system in DnD (though probably with more axis).  Things you do in game move you around on that axis.  Then you try to create content to create a sufficiently rich representation of different types of players.  Man, thats cool, but a lot of work.   How many of are there, deciding to try to make the cool feature that scares triple A studios?  Not trying to discourage you.  

One thing, most people have a type.  When they play your game, they will choose a play style and stick with it.  So the vast majority of the connections that players actually experience will be straightforward.  The cross connections, for when a play changes from chaotic evil to chaotic good, or something, will be far more rare.  In this example, less rare for the chaotic style (the nature of chaos), but still, it means a vast majority of the work will be seen by a very small minority of players.  

So what your wanting to do is give that work to an AI.  I think it will be very hard to maintain consistency in the AIs generated connection story.  You could lower the temperature, so it doesnt get to creative, but that might backfire too.  Then you have to make sure the AI doesnt lose context, so it's story doesnt contradict itself, or forget something that the player finds important.  You could have it create a document that tracks important story beats every time the story progresses.  That would have to be carefully prompted.  You would have to prompt it how to determine what is a "important story detail" and what isn't.  And you would need to do it as succinctly as possible.  

Are you building a prototype/ proof of concept, or just going for it?

Make sure you prompt the AI in exactly what vibe/tone the narrative should be.  Examples help, if they've been trained on the author.  Maybe even if they haven't, not sure on that one.  AI is getting pretty good even in situations where it doesnt have perfect training for.  I think.  

How far are you to being able to integrate an AI into your game?  Because if your not really close, the solution to your problem could change in the near future.

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body:
Haha fair, the original post was shorter than the explanation in the comments. Should have put more there.

And yeah I guess by your definition it is an AI. I just think of it differently since there is no LLM generating text. It is picking from hand written branches based on state matching. Feels more like a recommendation algorithm than what people normally call AI.

Good point about forced death. It is tricky to make it feel earned rather than arbitrary. Still figuring that part out.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body:
If you make the payoff awesome, the player will not only forgive you, but applaud you.  not consciously, but they will say "that was awesome" once you give the payoff.  They still wont like the loss of agency in a forced death, but that's the game of storytelling.  you have the manage the ebb and flow, highs and lows.  

I would suggest you edit the original post to make it more descriptive and clear... but you might already be to late.  Then against, this conversation just might give this post enough weight for the algorithm to put it high enough to get attention.  

My understanding of AI is anything that is predicting without just being a formula/algorithm.  I think that's right, but I'm not very confident.  That kind of AI has been around for a long time.  LLMs are the new shiny kids on the block.

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body: That is reassuring. I think the key is making the forced moment feel like a natural consequence rather than a cutscene. If the player can look back and go 'yeah that was inevitable given what I did' it lands differently than 'the game decided I die now'.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body: What death means also matters.  Like, how much does dying suck?  If they can die but that's not game over, then there must be some kind of respawn system.  How punishing is it?  If death is to inconsequential, you could well have the opposite problem.  Oh no, the story took a turn and my character died.  Who cares.  Good luck getting it right.  I'm cheering for you

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body:
Yeah that’s exactly the tension point.

The game I’m working on is called *One Day Rebirth*. The idea is you keep rebirthing into different characters inside a stable world, so you’re not just following one linear story — you’re experiencing the same world from different angles.

Death isn’t “game over”, but it also shouldn’t feel meaningless. It just becomes another branch in the world’s causality. The system tracks what led to it and what changes because of it, including NPC decisions that weren’t fully deterministic.

Over time I want to reconstruct and extend those causal chains, so even off-screen or “random” actions still feed back into the narrative.

So the player isn’t really chasing a win condition or leveling up — it’s more about slowly understanding how the world actually runs, like observing a living system rather than clearing a story.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body: That's a pretty cool twist.  But it's not enough of a story hook.  It's more like a interesting sauce than the main dish, know what I'm saying?  I assume you've already come up with a general narrative structure.  Since the story seems to be so central to this games identity, have you done research on the theory of storytelling?

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body:
I think you actually pointed right at the core of the idea.

The whole point of this game is trying to make that “interesting sauce” become the main dish.

Like imagine you play as the hero and kill a monster. Then in the next life, you rebirth as that monster. Suddenly the entire meaning of the world changes.

The goal is really to experience the same world from completely different perspectives and roles, so the world becomes more layered the longer you play.

And from a production side, that’s also why I’m interested in this structure. The maps, characters, items, and assets mostly stay the same. What keeps expanding is the story complexity and the relationships between events and characters.

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body: Death is not game over in my setup, it is a transition. You come back as a different person but keep your memories and some abilities. The death itself happens at sunset each day, it is a fixed point in the loop. So it is not like you failed a run, more like a chapter ended. That changes the emotional weight a lot.

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body:
Yeah, I probably explained the “director” part badly in the original post.

The game still runs on a stable main world, stable lore, and a stable core timeline. I’m not trying to make fully unconstrained AI storytelling.

The game theme is basically “one day loop”. Each loop is a different timeline, sometimes even from a different character’s perspective. Kind of like experiencing the same world from different angles.

The “director system” is more like a runtime rule system generated around that main storyline/world setup.

So each world setting / main narrative gets its own logic-driven director program. The goal of the runtime system is mostly to keep the core narrative structure coherent while allowing variation inside it.

The side branches are intentionally short and focused. More like roguelike encounter rooms than massive branching RPG narratives.

For example:

* getting an important item
* surviving a specific event
* helping or betraying someone
* escaping an area
* changing the outcome of a scene

Stuff like that.

So I’m not trying to generate infinite fully dynamic stories at runtime. That would probably collapse under its own weight pretty fast.

It’s more like controlled procedural narrative spaces inside a fixed world structure.

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body:
Yeah, and just to add one more thing.

There won’t be just one “director system”.

There are multiple director programs, basically different world versions running in parallel.

These worlds can have crossover points.

Depending on player behavior and preferences, the game can shift you into different director systems or timelines.

So it’s still one core world, but multiple controlled narrative layers on top of it.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body:
When you say they are running in parallel, they are running in game at the exact same time?  Or do you mean, like, they co exist in the code?  Will you be simulating what's happening in the other world versions when they are not the world version the player is engaging with?  
  
Sorry I keep challenging you on this, but what is your ultimate goal for this game?  The ultimate vision?  Do you want to tell a interesting story that's different for different kinds of players?  Is there this idea in your head that you just want to make, and everything else is secondary?

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body:
The discussion’s actually been really helpful, so thanks for pushing on the idea.

What I really want is for players to experience the same world through different characters, so the world starts feeling bigger and more layered instead of just “the player’s story”.

Like maybe in one loop you kill a monster, but later you rebirth as that monster and suddenly the whole world looks different from its side.

That shift in perspective is the part I’m most interested in.

So for me it’s less about making infinite content, and more about making the same world feel different depending on who you are, what you know, and what already happened.

Also from a development side, the workload is a bit different from normal RPGs. The maps, characters, items, and assets mostly stay the same. The thing that keeps growing is the story logic, NPC behavior, and the causal relationships between events.

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body:
One thing I’ve realized recently from talking with people on Reddit is that players already have very fixed expectations for certain genres.

Like when people hear “roguelike”, “RPG”, or “time loop game”, they immediately expect specific progression systems, pacing, rewards, and structure.

But the thing I’m trying to make sits somewhere in between genres, so sometimes I’m not even sure if it fits what people expect from an indie game.

A lot of the design is intentionally slower and more observational. The fun isn’t really “winning” or optimizing builds, it’s slowly understanding a world from different lives and perspectives.

So lately I’ve been thinking a lot about whether this idea is actually suited for a small indie project, or if it’s just too weird and experimental.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body:
I think Indie is the place where people expect the most experimentation.  

Don't internalize the friction here.  Use it to refine the idea.  Grind it down into the perfect gemstone.  

But the core of the idea could easily live in any number of media.  Visual novel, animation, one of those choice narrative games like Detroit: Become Human.

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body: Thanks, that is genuinely encouraging. The friction here has actually been useful for refining the pitch. Every time someone pushes back I realize I was explaining it wrong. Appreciate you sticking with the conversation.

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body:
yeah you’re right

no matter what the final format is, the core idea stays the same

what I’m really building is a director-driven system on top of causal data

the game, visual novel, animation, even interactive narrative stuff like Detroit-style games… they’re all just different shells for the same thing

the real value is in the runtime “director + world state + causality graph” loop

once that part works, the medium becomes flexible

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body: I still don't like calling it a director, unless it's more complex than what I got from your description.  Left 4 dead had a director.  This just sounds like you're choosing content based on variables provided by the players behavior.  Then again if you're trying to sell your game the word director does sound good.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
it is not hard to do if you embed a local AI in your game but it is probably an overkill

not sure if you already have the choices/dialogue planned out but you will need enough choices/dialogue for players to be able to build distinct player history.

think about it this way: you can set up your game with your approach as you described or you can just give the player a random choice. If the two results aren't all that different most of the time, then the whole setup is a waste of effort.

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body: Yeah local AI might be overkill for my case. The choices and dialogue are pre-written, the director just picks what to surface based on player state. Kind of like a recommendation engine more than an AI.
